props.title: Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice

sections.content: Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice (1969) revolutionized Hollywood's treatment of sexual politics and marriage. Director Paul Mazursky captured the exact moment California's encounter group culture collided with middle-class sexual mores. Like The Graduate (1967) and Carnal Knowledge (1971), it exposed the fault lines in American sexual attitudes, but did so through sophisticated comedy rather than drama. The film's genius lies in showing how Bob and Carol's newfound "enlightenment" creates ripple effects of jealousy, curiosity, and confusion among their more conventional friends.

sections.content: The film's influence echoed through 1970s cinema, inspiring a wave of relationship comedies that dealt frankly with marriage and sexuality. Shampoo (1975) borrowed its LA setting and sexual politics, while An Unmarried Woman (1978) expanded on its feminist themes. The film's iconic ending - four leads in bed together who can't go through with partner-swapping - perfectly captured America's simultaneous fascination with and resistance to sexual revolution ideals.

Mazursky's direction feels remarkably modern, avoiding both moralistic judgment and exploitation. The naturalistic performances, especially from Natalie Wood and Elliott Gould, ground the potentially sensational material in relatable human behavior. Like Marriage Story (2019) or Scenes from a Marriage (1973), the film uses relationship dynamics to explore deeper truths about intimacy, honesty, and social change. sections.content: The film kicked off a decade of more explicit exploration of sexuality in mainstream American cinema. Last Tango in Paris (1972) pushed boundaries with its raw depiction of sexual obsession, while Paul Mazursky's next film Blume in Love (1973) continued examining marriage in the age of liberation. The film's influence can be seen in modern works like The Ice Storm (1997) and Little Children (2006), which similarly explore suburban sexual experimentation.
